content:
A Missouri judge has approved Bayer's $7.25 billion settlement of lawsuits alleging that its weedkiller Roundup causes cancer, a decision that could finally bring to a close litigation that has weighed on the German company for almost a decade. St. Louis Circuit Judge Timothy Boyer granted final approval on Friday, November 20, finding the nationwide class settlement "fair, reasonable, and adequate" and describing the total as among the largest in the history of mass tort personal-injury class action settlements, according to [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/missouri-judge-approves-bayers-725-billion-roundup-settlement-2026-11-20/).

The settlement, first announced in February, aims to resolve nearly all current and future Roundup claims in the United States. Bayer is facing approximately 65,000 claims in US state and federal courts from people who say they developed non-Hodgkin lymphoma, a form of cancer, after using Roundup at home or at work. Under the deal, Monsanto will make declining capped annual payments for up to 21 years, totalling as much as $7.25 billion, including payments already made. Individual payouts will range from $10,000 to $165,000, depending on the severity of the person's illness, how old they were when diagnosed, and whether they were exposed to the weedkiller at home or at work.

Crucially, the agreement covers not only people who are already ill but also those who fall sick in the future. It creates two subclasses: people who were exposed to Roundup before February 17, 2026 and already have a diagnosis of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and people who receive such a diagnosis within a 16-year period after final approval. The long-term claims programme will resolve present and future injury claims regardless of the legal theory on which they are based, giving both sides something the courts have so far failed to deliver: certainty. The approved settlement also includes $600 million for attorneys' fees, and the court's final approval order is subject to appeal.

Judge Boyer rejected numerous objections to the deal, including arguments from opponents that it does not offer enough money and is designed to trap current and future claimants who would prefer to pursue their lawsuits in court. In his written judgment, he warned that there was a risk Bayer would have filed for bankruptcy protection if the settlement had been rejected, a scenario in which claimants might have received far less, or nothing at all. Lawyers for plaintiffs who support the settlement have made the same point, saying the deal ensures that people with cancer will actually get paid at a time when litigation has become more uncertain than ever.

That uncertainty grew sharply in June, when the US Supreme Court ruled 7-2 in the Durnell case that the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act preempts "failure-to-warn" claims brought in state court, undercutting a central argument in many of the lawsuits. The settlement approval followed closely on a unanimous defence verdict in the Aretino case, the first to go to trial since the Durnell decision. Together, the Supreme Court ruling and the Aretino verdict strengthened Bayer's hand considerably, and the company says the two developments are mutually reinforcing pillars of its strategy to contain the litigation. About 200 lawsuits consolidated in an ongoing federal court proceeding are excluded from the settlement, and Bayer says the Supreme Court's ruling gives it strong defences in those cases.

Bayer chief executive Bill Anderson called the court-approved settlement "a decisive milestone in the company's strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation." For Bayer, the stakes could hardly be higher. The litigation has dogged the company since its $63 billion acquisition of Monsanto in 2018, costing it billions of dollars and driving down its share price. Bayer previously spent about $10 billion in 2020 to resolve most of the lawsuits that existed at the time, but it was unable to gain court approval for a parallel $1.25 billion settlement that would have resolved future claims. The mounting legal costs had even led the company to contemplate pulling Roundup from US agricultural markets.

Bayer continues to deny that Roundup causes cancer, saying decades of studies have shown that its key ingredient, glyphosate, is safe. Regulators around the world have reached differing conclusions: the US Environmental Protection Agency has said glyphosate is not likely to be carcinogenic to humans, while the World Health Organization's International Agency for Research on Cancer classified it in 2015 as "probably carcinogenic to humans." That scientific divide is at the heart of why the litigation has proved so hard to settle, and why a court-approved structure for future claims matters so much to both sides.

The approval does not end every question. The decision can be appealed, and objectors may challenge the terms. But if it stands, it gives Bayer the financial predictability it has sought for eight years, gives tens of thousands of claimants a defined route to compensation without years of further litigation, and sets a template for how courts handle mass claims where the science remains contested. Large corporate settlements of this kind are increasingly decided not by a single trial verdict but by negotiated programmes that stretch over decades, as [Rio Tinto's $250 million legacy fund for the Panguna mine](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/rio-tinto-250-million-panguna-mine-legacy-fund-november-2026) showed earlier this month. For farmers, gardeners and Bayer's shareholders alike, the message from the St. Louis courtroom is that the Roundup litigation, which has shaped the company's strategy and its share price for the better part of a decade, is finally nearing its end, even as the debate over glyphosate itself continues. Bayer's $7.25 billion deal is also one of the largest corporate settlements of the year, in a period of major dealmaking that has included [TPG and Corpay's $6 billion buyout](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/tpg-corpay-bill-6-billion-buyout-november-2026).
summary: A Missouri judge has given final approval to Bayer's $7.25 billion nationwide settlement resolving nearly all current and future US lawsuits alleging its Roundup weedkiller causes cancer, ending a legal battle that has weighed on the German company since its 2018 purchase of Monsanto.
title: Missouri judge approves Bayer's $7.25 billion Roundup settlement, closing a decade of cancer litigation
